lessons.title: Temperature and Humidity Management
lessons.body: Temperature and humidity are the most critical environmental factors for broiler health and growth. Day-old chicks need a brooding temperature of 32-34Â°C at chick level. Reduce by 2-3Â°C each week until 20-22Â°C at 4-5 weeks. In Africa, use a thermometer at chick height. For heating, use charcoal stoves, gas brooders, or infrared bulbs. In hot climates, open curtains, use fans, and sprinkle water on the roof. Humidity should be 60-70% in the first week, then 50-60%. High humidity with high temperature causes heat stress; low humidity causes dehydration. Use a hygrometer. In dry areas, hang wet sacks or use misters. In humid coastal areas, increase ventilation. Monitor chicks: if they huddle under heat, they are cold; if they pant and spread out, they are hot. Adjust accordingly. Always provide cool, clean water. In extreme heat, add electrolytes. In cold, avoid drafts but allow fresh air. Record daily temperature and humidity to track patterns. Power outages are common; have backup heating. For small flocks, use a kerosene lamp inside a metal drum for emergency heat. Remember, day-old chicks cannot regulate their own body temperature for the first two weeks, so you must be their thermostat.

lessons.title: Air Quality and Ammonia Control
lessons.body: Ammonia gas from litter burns birds' eyes and lungs, causing blindness, respiratory disease, and poor growth. If you smell ammonia at human nose level, it is already too high for birds (above 25 ppm). Aim for less than 20 ppm. To control ammonia: remove wet litter, increase ventilation, and use litter amendments like superphosphate (0.5 kg per mÂ²) or zeolite. In open-sided houses, adjust curtains to allow airflow without drafts. In tunnels, ensure fans pull air from one end to the other. Never block vents to keep heat in; stale air is worse than cold. Check ammonia levels with a handheld meter or your nose. If your eyes water, act immediately. Also, carbon dioxide and dust are concerns. Dust from feed and feathers can cause respiratory issues. Use pelleted feed to reduce dust, and avoid overstocking. Stocking density: maximum 10-12 birds per mÂ² in open houses, 15-18 in controlled. In Africa, many farms are open-sided; use ridge vents and side curtains. During hot weather, open all vents. During cold, open only top vents. Stir litter daily to release trapped gases. If using gas brooders, ensure proper combustion; faulty heaters produce carbon monoxide. Never use charcoal stoves in sealed rooms. Provide fresh air without chilling chicks. A simple test: if you can see your breath, it's too cold and humid; if you cough, ammonia is high.

lessons.title: Litter Management and Moisture Control
lessons.body: Litter is the bedding on the floor. Good litter absorbs moisture, provides cushioning, and dilutes manure. Use wood shavings, rice hulls, or chopped straw. Avoid sawdust (too fine) and sand (too abrasive). Spread 5-10 cm deep. Litter should be dry and crumbly, not wet or caked. Wet litter causes ammonia, breast blisters, and footpad dermatitis. To control moisture: fix drinkers immediately. Use nipple drinkers or closed cups to prevent spillage. If using open drinkers, place them on raised platforms. Increase ventilation to remove moisture. In humid areas, add fresh litter regularly. Turn litter daily to aerate. If litter gets wet, remove clumps and add dry material. A simple test: squeeze a handful; it should not drip water. If it does, it's too wet. Litter moisture should be 20-25%. In Africa, many farmers use deep litter. To prevent caking, avoid overstocking and ensure drinkers are not too close to feeders. When litter becomes too wet, it can be replaced entirely, but that is costly. Instead, maintain it. After each flock, remove all litter, clean and disinfect, then add new litter. Used litter is good fertilizer for crops. Never let litter get too dry and dusty; that causes respiratory problems. Aim for a balance: not too wet, not too dry. Check litter daily by walking through the house; if it sticks to your boots, it's too wet.

lessons.title: Lighting Intensity and Duration Adjustments
lessons.body: Light controls feeding, growth, and reproduction. Broilers need light to find feed and water. For the first 7 days, provide 23 hours of light and 1 hour of darkness. Use 40-60 watt bulbs per 20 mÂ², hung 2-2.5 m high. Intensity should be bright enough to read a newspaper. After day 7, reduce to 20 hours of light and 4 hours of dark, or use intermittent lighting (e.g., 1 hour light, 2 hours dark) to save energy and reduce stress. In Africa, natural daylight may be enough in open houses, but supplemental light is needed in the morning and evening. Use LED bulbs to save power. Avoid sudden changes in lighting; it stresses birds. Keep light uniform; shadows cause crowding. Clean bulbs regularly; dust reduces output. In hot climates, provide light during cooler hours (early morning, late evening) so birds eat when it's cool. For heavy breeds, longer light increases feed intake and weight. For leanness, shorter light. But never go below 18 hours total light in the first 3 weeks. After 3 weeks, you can use 18 hours light, 6 hours dark. Some farmers use 12 hours light, 12 hours dark from day 21 to reduce sudden death syndrome. Always observe birds: if they are not eating, check lighting. If they are panting, reduce light intensity. Use a timer to automate. In areas with power cuts, use solar-powered lights or rechargeable lamps. Remember, darkness allows birds to rest and grow.

lessons.title: Noise and Stress Reduction
lessons.body: Noise stresses broilers, leading to reduced feed intake, poor growth, and increased disease. Sudden loud noises cause panic, crowding, and injury. Common sources: vehicles, generators, dogs, shouting, and equipment. Minimize noise by locating houses away from roads and noisy activities. Use sound barriers like trees or walls. Train workers to move calmly and speak softly. Avoid banging doors or dropping equipment. Turn off radios and loud machines. In open houses, noise from outside is hard to control, but you can mask it with soft background music? No, that may add noise. Better to reduce. Handle birds gently during vaccination or weighing. Use dim light during handling to keep them calm. Keep a routine: feed, water, and check at the same times daily. Birds thrive on predictability. If a noise occurs, don't panic; move slowly. Provide hiding spots? Not practical. Instead, ensure enough space so birds can spread out. Stocking density affects stress: overcrowding amplifies noise stress. Keep density at 10-12 birds/mÂ². In hot climates, noise plus heat is deadly. So during heat stress, minimize all disturbances. If you must move birds, do it at night. Use fans that are quiet. Fix squeaky doors. Train dogs to stay away. If you have children, keep them away from houses. Stress increases cortisol, which suppresses immunity. So, a quiet farm is a healthy farm. Also, consider the noise from your own operations: feed mixing, generator, etc. Schedule noisy tasks when birds are least active, or use ear protection for birds? No, just reduce noise at source. A simple test: stand inside the house; if it's uncomfortably loud, it's too loud for birds.

lessons.title: Waste Management and Environmental Impact
lessons.body: Broiler waste includes litter, manure, dead birds, and wastewater. Improper disposal pollutes soil, water, and air, and spreads disease. Manage waste to protect the environment and earn extra income. Litter and manure are valuable fertilizers. After each flock, remove litter, compost it, and sell to crop farmers. Composting: pile litter, keep moist, turn weekly for 4-6 weeks. This kills pathogens and weed seeds. Use compost on gardens or sell in bags. Dead birds: never throw in rivers or bushes. Use incineration, burial, or composting. Incinerators must be far from houses. Burial pits should be 1.5 m deep, covered with lime. Composting dead birds: layer with litter and straw, turn regularly. This is safe and produces fertilizer. Wastewater from cleaning: don't dump into streams. Use a soak pit or constructed wetland. In Africa, water is scarce, so recycle where possible. Reduce waste by using nipple drinkers (less spillage) and proper feed storage. Avoid overstocking to reduce waste volume. Also, consider flies and odours: keep litter dry, use fly traps, and plant aromatic herbs like lemongrass around houses. Environmental impact: broiler farming contributes to greenhouse gases (methane, nitrous oxide) from manure. Proper composting reduces emissions. Also, avoid antibiotics in feed; use alternatives. Finally, comply with local regulations. Many African countries have laws on waste disposal. Check with extension officers. A clean farm is a profitable farm. Sell compost as organic fertilizer; it's in demand. Use dead birds for biogas? Possible but requires investment. Start simple: compost and sell. This turns waste into wealth.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Environmental Control for Broiler Farming in Africa

Environmental control is the single most profitable management lever in a broiler house. In African conditions â high ambient temperatures, seasonal harmattan dust, unreliable grid power, and humid coastal zones â the difference between a 1.6 kg and a 2.3 kg bird at 35 days is usually not feed quality. It is the environment: temperature, humidity, air quality, litter moisture, light, noise, and waste handling. This Practical Reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into field-ready targets, tables, and checklists. Treat it as your daily operating standard, not a theoretical guide.

Business logic: Every 1% improvement in feed conversion ratio (FCR) on a 5,000-bird flock saves roughly 75â100 kg of feed per cycle. At USD 0.45/kg, that is USD 34â45 per cycle â before you count reduced mortality, lower medication costs, and higher carcass grade. Environmental control pays for itself within one or two cycles when implemented systematically.

1. Temperature and Humidity Management

Day-old chicks cannot thermoregulate. Set the brooding temperature at 32â34Â°C at chick level for days 1â3, then reduce by 2â3Â°C per week until 20â22Â°C at day 21â28. Relative humidity should sit between 60â70% in the first week and 50â65% thereafter. In the Sahel and East African highlands, night temperatures can fall 15Â°C below daytime â plan supplementary heating (gas brooders, charcoal stoves with safe flues, or infrared lamps) and backup power for fans.

Source: Aviagen Broiler Management Handbook (2023); Cobb500 Broiler Management Guide (2022).

2. Air Quality and Ammonia Control

Ammonia (NHâ) above 20 ppm damages the respiratory tract, reduces feed intake, and predisposes birds to colibacillosis and CRD. In poorly ventilated African houses, NHâ can exceed 50 ppm within 10 days. Target: NHâ < 20 ppm, COâ < 3,000 ppm, and no detectable dust haze. If your eyes sting on entry, the birds are already under stress.

Table 2: Air quality thresholds and corrective actions

Ammonia (NHâ)< 20 ppm> 25 ppmIncrease ventilation, add litter, remove wet patches
Carbon dioxide (COâ)< 3,000 ppm> 4,000 ppmOpen inlets, check fan function
DustLowVisible hazeSprinkle litter lightly, improve airflow
Air velocity (hot weather)0.5â1.5 m/s< 0.3 m/sAdd fans or tunnel ventilation

Source: FAO Poultry Housing Guidelines (2008); Aviagen Broiler Management Handbook (2023).

3. Litter Management and Moisture Control

Litter is your cheapest environmental tool. Maintain 5â8 cm of dry, friable material â wood shavings, rice husks, or chopped maize cobs are common in Africa. Target moisture 20â25%. Above 30%, ammonia release and footpad dermatitis rise sharply. Stir litter daily in the first two weeks and spot-remove wet patches around drinkers. In humid coastal zones (Mombasa, Lagos, Accra), increase ventilation and use raised drinker stands to reduce spillage.

4. Lighting Intensity and Duration Adjustments

Use 23 hours of light at 20â30 lux for days 1â7 to encourage feeding. From day 8, drop to 18â20 hours at 5â10 lux. This reduces activity, improves FCR, and lowers heat stress. In areas with unreliable power, use solar-powered LED bulbs â a 9W LED per 20 mÂ² is sufficient. Dark periods of 4â6 hours improve leg health and reduce sudden death syndrome.

5. Noise and Stress Reduction

Broilers are sensitive to sudden noise â generator starts, barking dogs, loud music, or shouting. Chronic stress raises corticosterone, suppresses immunity, and lowers weight gain by 5â10%. Site houses away from roads and markets. Fix loose iron sheets that rattle. Train workers to move slowly and speak quietly. In areas near mosques, churches, or markets, use sound barriers (hedges, walls) and schedule noisy operations outside peak stress periods.

6. Waste Management and Environmental Impact

Poultry litter is not waste â it is a revenue stream. Compost it for 4â6 weeks to kill pathogens, then sell as organic fertiliser to vegetable farmers (USD 3â8 per 50 kg bag in many African markets). Dead birds must be disposed of by deep burial, incineration, or composting â never thrown into rivers or open pits. Wash water from the house should be directed to a soak pit or used on fodder plots, not discharged into streams. Check local environmental regulations, especially in peri-urban areas.

â  SAFETY WARNING:

Never enter a closed broiler house with a running generator or charcoal brooder without ventilation. Carbon monoxide and ammonia can reach lethal levels within minutes. Always open inlets and run fans for 10 minutes before entry. When using gas brooders, install a CO monitor and keep a fire extinguisher at the door. In Africa, generator exhaust must be piped outside the house â never allow exhaust into the bird area. Fumigation chemicals and formalin are hazardous: wear gloves, goggles, and a respirator, and never fumigate with birds inside.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check chick behaviour three times daily â huddling (cold), panting (hot), or even spread (correct).
  2. Record temperature and humidity at chick level morning, noon, and night.
  3. Smell the air on entry â if your eyes sting, NHâ is above 20 ppm; ventilate immediately.
  4. Stir litter daily for the first 14 days; remove wet patches around drinkers.
  5. Verify light hours and intensity match the age schedule; replace flickering bulbs.
  6. Inspect fans, inlets, and ridge vents weekly; clean dust from fan blades.
  7. Keep a noise log â note generator starts, markets, or events that stress birds.
  8. Compost litter and dispose of dead birds by approved methods; never dump in waterways.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Aviagen Broiler Management Handbook (2023) â comprehensive environmental control tables.
  • Cobb500 Broiler Management Guide â temperature, humidity, and lighting schedules.
  • FAO: Poultry Development Review â housing, waste management, and biosecurity in developing countries.
  • FAO: Good Practices for the Meat Industry â environmental impact and waste handling.
  • WOAH Terrestrial Animal Health Code â welfare and housing standards for poultry.

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Broiler Farming Module: Environmental Control. Always adapt targets to your local climate, breed, and market requirements.

quiz.q: What is the recommended brooding temperature for day-old chicks?
quiz.explanation: Day-old chicks need 32-34Â°C at chick level for proper warmth and development.

quiz.q: How can you tell if chicks are too cold?
options: A) They pant and spread out
B) They huddle together under the heat source
quiz.explanation: Huddling indicates chicks are trying to conserve heat because they are cold.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for broilers in the first week?
quiz.explanation: 60-70% humidity prevents dehydration and respiratory issues in young chicks.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to measure humidity?
quiz.explanation: A hygrometer measures relative humidity in the air.

quiz.q: What is the maximum acceptable ammonia level in a broiler house?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia should be kept below 20 ppm to prevent respiratory damage.

quiz.q: Which litter material is recommended for broilers?
quiz.explanation: Wood shavings are absorbent, soft, and safe for broiler litter.

quiz.q: What is the ideal litter moisture content?
quiz.explanation: 20-25% moisture keeps litter dry and crumbly, reducing ammonia and disease.

quiz.q: How can you reduce ammonia in the broiler house?
quiz.explanation: Superphosphate acidifies litter and reduces ammonia release.

quiz.q: What is the recommended light duration for broilers in the first week?
quiz.explanation: 23 hours light and 1 hour dark helps chicks find feed and water initially.

quiz.q: Why is it important to have a dark period for broilers?
options: B) To allow rest and reduce stress
quiz.explanation: Dark periods allow birds to rest, which improves growth and reduces stress.

quiz.q: What is the recommended light intensity for broilers?
options: A) Very dim, just enough to see
B) Bright enough to read a newspaper
quiz.explanation: Bright enough to read a newspaper ensures birds can find feed and water.

quiz.q: Which of these is a source of noise stress in broiler houses?
quiz.explanation: Generators produce loud, sudden noises that stress birds.

quiz.q: How can you reduce noise stress?
options: B) Move calmly and speak softly
quiz.explanation: Calm movements and soft speech minimize sudden noises that scare birds.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in broilers?
quiz.explanation: Panting and spreading out are attempts to lose heat when too hot.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stocking density for broilers in open houses?
quiz.explanation: 10-12 birds/mÂ² prevents overcrowding and stress in open-sided houses.

quiz.q: How should dead birds be disposed of?
quiz.explanation: Burying or incinerating dead birds prevents disease spread and environmental pollution.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of composting litter?
options: A) It kills pathogens and produces fertilizer
quiz.explanation: Composting heats up, killing pathogens and creating nutrient-rich fertilizer.

quiz.q: Which drinker type reduces litter moisture?
quiz.explanation: Nipple drinkers prevent spillage, keeping litter dry.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for wet litter?
options: A) Squeeze a handful; if it drips, it's too wet
quiz.explanation: If water drips when squeezed, litter moisture is too high.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sudden changes in lighting?
quiz.explanation: Sudden lighting changes cause stress and panic in broilers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a dark period in broiler lighting?
options: B) To allow rest and prevent metabolic disorders
D) To make birds more active
quiz.explanation: Dark periods allow rest, reducing stress and metabolic issues like ascites.

quiz.q: Which gas is produced by decomposing litter and is harmful to birds?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia is released from uric acid in manure and damages respiratory tracts.

quiz.q: How can you improve air quality without chilling chicks?
options: D) Use fans directly on chicks
quiz.explanation: Top vents allow stale air to escape without creating cold drafts at chick level.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good air quality?
options: B) No smell and clear air
quiz.explanation: No ammonia smell indicates good ventilation and low gas levels.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth of litter?
quiz.explanation: 5-10 cm of litter provides adequate absorption and cushioning.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good practice for litter management?
quiz.explanation: Turning litter aerates it, preventing caking and reducing ammonia.

quiz.q: What is the environmental impact of improper waste disposal?
quiz.explanation: Improper disposal pollutes water sources and releases harmful gases.

quiz.q: How can you reduce noise from equipment?
quiz.explanation: Regular maintenance reduces squeaks and loud noises from equipment.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for broilers at 4-5 weeks?
quiz.explanation: By 4-5 weeks, broilers need 20-22Â°C for optimal growth.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to increase humidity in a broiler house?
quiz.explanation: Wet sacks evaporate water, raising humidity in dry conditions.
